findings.paper_title: 260713 Collection of Council Tax, Business Rates and Rent 2025-26
findings.headline: Council writing off £1.22 million of irrecoverable debts across all revenue streams
findings.detail: Total write-offs approved for 2025-26 amount to £1,215,433 across Council Tax (£450k), Business Rates (£320k), former council rent arrears (£156k), Housing Benefit overpayments (£51k) and sundry debts (£239k). Council Tax alone saw additional write-offs of £718,539 for debts under £1,000.
findings.matters: High write-off volumes indicate a significant proportion of assessed debts are unrecoverable, reducing effective revenue collection and potentially signalling deteriorating creditworthiness of the local population or businesses.
findings.figures: Total write-offs over £1,000: £1,215,433; Council Tax under £1,000: £718,539; total net Council Tax write-off: £886,762
findings.quote: Approval is being sought to write-off a total of £1,215,433 of debts in respect of individual cases exceeding £1,000 for the financial year 2025-26, where it has become apparent that no further steps can be taken to recover the sums due

findings.paper_title: 260713 Collection of Council Tax, Business Rates and Rent 2025-26
findings.headline: Sundry debts outstanding jumped £3.2 million to £14.75 million with only 92.3% collection rate
findings.detail: Outstanding sundry debts increased sharply from £11.552 million to £14.750 million, a jump of £3.2 million. Collection of new sundry debts in 2025-26 was only £41.051 million out of £44.495 million raised (92.3%), the weakest collection rate of all revenue types.
findings.matters: Growing sundry debt stock indicates accumulating receivables that may become irrecoverable; the 92.3% collection rate is significantly below Council Tax and Business Rates, suggesting service areas struggle to collect from customers.
findings.figures: Outstanding sundry debts: £14.750m (March 2026) vs £11.552m (March 2025); collection rate 92.3%
findings.quote: During 2025-26, a total of £44.495 million of new sundry debts were raised and £41.051 million was collected (or 92.3%). Therefore, the amount of outstanding sundry debts has increased from £11.552 million in March 2025 to £14.750 million in March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 260713 Collection of Council Tax, Business Rates and Rent 2025-26
findings.headline: Council rent arrears grew 20% to £1.06 million due to structural shift from Housing Benefit to Universal Credit
findings.detail: Council rent arrears increased from £880,829 to £1,061,259 between April 2025 and April 2026. The document explicitly states this is due to managed migration of working age tenants from Housing Benefit (paid weekly in advance) to Universal Credit (paid monthly in arrears), creating a structural cash flow mismatch.
findings.matters: This is a structural, ongoing issue not temporary economic weakness. The UC payment cycle creates a permanent arrears bulge that will require ongoing collection effort and may require housing revenue account provisions.
findings.figures: Rent arrears: £1,061,259 (April 2026) vs £880,829 (April 2025); increase of £180,430 (20.5%)
findings.quote: However, the amount of rent arrears has increased from £880,829 in April 2025 to £1,061,259 in April 2026. The increase in rent arrears can largely be attributed to the managed migration of working age Council tenants from Housing Benefit to Universal Credit.

findings.paper_title: 260713 Collection of Council Tax, Business Rates and Rent 2025-26
findings.headline: Business Rates collection fell from 99.2% to 98.4% and arrears nearly doubled to £1.06 million
findings.detail: Business Rates collection declined from 99.2% in 2024-25 to 98.4% in 2025-26. Business Rates arrears increased 41% from £0.75 million in March 2025 to £1.06 million in March 2026. This is the fastest-growing arrears category and suggests weakness in the local business base.
findings.matters: Business Rates volatility indicates economic weakness in the local area; rising arrears may signal business distress or failure to pay, both precursors to declining local tax base.
findings.figures: Collection rate fell from 99.2% (2024-25) to 98.4% (2025-26); arrears £1.06m (March 2026) vs £0.75m (March 2025)
findings.quote: During 2025-26, a total of £36.73 million of Business Rates was due, of which £36.15 million was collected (or 98.4%). This compares to £34.06 million collected in 2024-25 (or 99.2%). Business Rates arrears have increased from £0.75 million in March 2025 to £1.06 million in March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 260713 Collection of Council Tax, Business Rates and Rent 2025-26
findings.headline: Council Tax collection rate fell to 96.6%, the lowest in the reporting period since 2012-13
findings.detail: Council Tax collection dropped from 97.5% in 2024-25 to 96.6% in 2025-26. Tax arrears increased from £6.55 million to £6.79 million in the same period. The historical table shows a consistent downward trend: collection rates fell from 98.9% in 2019-20 to 96.6% in 2025-26.
findings.matters: Council Tax is a core predictable revenue source; a declining collection rate signals weakening income generation and may indicate emerging affordability pressures in the council area.
findings.figures: Collection rate 96.6% in 2025-26 vs 97.5% in 2024-25; arrears £6.79m (March 2026) vs £6.55m (March 2025)
findings.quote: During 2025-26, a total of £85.54 million of Council Tax was due, of which £82.56 million was collected (or 96.5%). In addition, £1.65 million of Council Tax arrears relating to previous years was collected in 2025-26.

findings.paper_title: Annual Risk Management Report 2025 2026
findings.headline: Business Continuity Plans were inadequately reviewed for cyber incident preparedness, with the review deadline having just passed at the time of this report.
findings.detail: The Civil Contingencies Unit ran a session on 3 June 2026 asking lead officers to reflect on their preparedness for cyber incidents. This led to Risk SR3 being increased. Lead officers were tasked with reviewing Business Continuity Plans 'to ensure they are as prepared as reasonably practicable for dealing with a cyber incident,' with a deadline of 17 July 2026 (the week after this report). The plans will then be audited by the Contingencies Unit.
findings.matters: If a major cyber incident occurs while business continuity planning is inadequate, the council could be unable to deliver critical services including social care, electoral services, benefit payments and council tax collection. This creates operational and therefore financial risk.
findings.figures: Deadline 17 July 2026; session held 3 June 2026
findings.quote: Lead officers have been tasked with reviewing their Business Continuity Plans (BCPs) in conjunction with CCU to ensure they are as prepared as reasonably practicable for dealing with a cyber incident. The deadline for doing so is 17 July

findings.paper_title: Annual Risk Management Report 2025 2026
findings.headline: High Court rulings on Ordinary Resident liability create a potential unfunded financial liability for adult social care costs.
findings.detail: Recent High Court rulings on Ordinary Resident cases create a risk to the council for financial liability for people under this new rule. The council has identified current cases and is working with other local authorities to agree responsibilities. A regional agreement has been reached with 10 of 13 local authorities for reciprocal arrangements, but the risk of liability for unallocated cases remains.
findings.matters: Legal changes that create unexpected financial liabilities undermine budget planning and can rapidly consume reserves or require emergency borrowing. The fact that regional agreements cover only 10 of 13 authorities suggests some councils may still face unallocated liability.
findings.figures: Regional agreement with 10 of 13 local authorities; specific case numbers not disclosed
findings.quote: Due to recent High Court rulings on Ordinary Resident cases there is a risk to the Council for financial liability for people under this new rule.

findings.paper_title: Annual Risk Management Report 2025 2026
findings.headline: The care provider market faces cost pressures from national employer insurance contributions and statutory sick pay changes, with the council providing additional subsidy.
findings.detail: National changes to Employers National Insurance Contributions (ENI) and Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) have created cost pressures for care providers. Fuel cost increases have also impacted parts of the provider market, particularly homecare services. The council has responded by providing 'additional financial support to providers (Market Sustainability and Improvement funding for travel costs and an additional 1.2% on current fee levels for ENI)' and continues to monitor provider stability.
findings.matters: Care provider instability creates two risks: either providers fail and the council must find alternative arrangements at emergency cost, or the council must continue subsidising providers to prevent failure. Either path drains the council's budget.
findings.figures: Additional 1.2% fee increase for ENI; Market Sustainability and Improvement funding for travel costs
findings.quote: The national changes to Employers National Insurance Contributions (ENI) and Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) have resulted in additional cost pressures to the care provider market. Fuel cost increases have also impacted on some areas of the provider market (particularly Homecare). The Council has provided additional financial support to providers

findings.paper_title: Annual Risk Management Report 2025 2026
findings.headline: Adult social care is experiencing waiting lists for reviews and assessments, and is dependent on short-term government funding to maintain current workforce capacity.
findings.detail: The council faces increasing demand for adult social care including domiciliary care, aides, adaptations and support for people with significant learning disabilities. Waiting lists exist for reviews and assessments. The council has increased workforce capacity 'through agency, additional hours and fixed term contracts to manage demand, however this is currently short-term funding' from the Department of Health and Social Care social discharge fund. The council continues to monitor demand versus capacity.
findings.matters: Short-term funding used to manage demand pressure signals the council has not found a sustainable solution to this structural problem. When temporary funding expires, the council will face a cliff-edge budget crisis unless demand falls or new funding materialises.
findings.figures: Unfunded capacity increases via agency and fixed-term contracts
findings.quote: With support from the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) social discharge fund we have increased workforce capacity through agency, additional hours and fixed term contracts to manage demand, however this is currently short-term funding.

findings.paper_title: Annual Risk Management Report 2025 2026
findings.headline: The council faces unrelenting demand pressure in children's and adult social care, where over a third of the council budget is committed.
findings.detail: The risk report describes the council facing 'significant and unparalleled financial challenges' with 'significant demand for services particularly in Children's and Adults Social Care, statutory services where over a third of the budget is spent to look after our most vulnerable residents and children.' The risk matrix shows increased demand for both children's services and adult services limiting the council's ability to fund other priorities.
findings.matters: Social care demand represents a structural budget problem beyond the council's control. When over a third of budget is committed to demand-led statutory services, discretionary spending and capital investment become vulnerable. Persistent demand growth threatens the viability of the savings plans.
findings.figures: Over one-third of total budget committed to Children's and Adult Social Care
findings.quote: The Council is facing significant demand for services particularly in Children's and Adults Social Care, statutory services where over a third of the budget is spent to look after our most vulnerable residents and children.

findings.paper_title: Annual Risk Management Report 2025 2026
findings.headline: The council will deploy approximately £8m of reserves over the first two years of the Medium Term Financial Plan to achieve a balanced budget.
findings.detail: The approved 2026/27–2029/30 MTFP includes £13m of savings but still requires the use of reserves of circa £8m in the first two years (2026/27 and 2027/28) before the council returns to modest surpluses from 2028/29. This indicates the savings plan alone is insufficient to close the budget gap.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is a key indicator of unsustainable budget positions. Lenders monitor reserves as a buffer against shortfalls; drawing them down to balance budgets signals reduced financial flexibility and increased borrowing risk.
findings.figures: £13m savings over four-year plan; £8m reserves deployed in first two years
findings.quote: includes savings of over £13m over the life of the plan which along with planned increases in Council Tax of 4.99% provides a balanced budget across of the life of the plan, using reserves of circa. £8m in the first two years, before returning to modest surpluses from 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Annual Risk Management Report 2025 2026
findings.headline: Auditors expect to issue a fourth consecutive disclaimer of opinion on the council's accounts for 2025/26.
findings.detail: Darlington has received disclaimer of opinions on 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25 accounts due to national audit delays. Auditors have informed the council they will not have time to complete required testing and a full audit of 2025/26 accounts before the January 2027 deadline, making another disclaimer likely. Audits may not return to normal until 2027/28.
findings.matters: Persistent disclaimer opinions signal severe governance and financial reporting issues that directly affect creditworthiness and lender confidence. Multiple years of unqualified audit opinions block transparency on the council's true financial position.
findings.figures: 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25 accounts issued with disclaimer; 2025/26 expected to follow; 2026/27 also at risk; expected to normalise 2027/28
findings.quote: Due to the timing of the release of the guidance and the need to test, our Auditors have informed that they will not have time to complete the proof in total work for the previously disclaimed audit years and undertake a full audit of the 2025/26 accounts, before the end of January 27 backstop deadline, therefore they have indicated that a disclaimed opinion is likely to be issued for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 260713 RBM Outturn 2025-26 Appendix 1
findings.headline: Financing Costs underspend by £834k—the single largest variance
findings.detail: Financing costs are projected £834k below the MTFP plan, representing 43% of the total £1.9m improvement in the reserve position. The driver is not explained in this appendix; it could reflect lower borrowing levels, refinancing gains, or changed interest rate assumptions.
findings.matters: Financing cost variances reveal debt management performance and borrowing position. A £834k underspend is material and could indicate structural improvements to debt sustainability, or could be a one-off benefit. Lenders assess this closely when evaluating future borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Financing Costs (834); Total improvement vs MTFP £1,935k
findings.quote: Financing Costs (834)

findings.paper_title: 260713 RG RBM Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's positive £1.935m year-end improvement masks ongoing structural budget challenge
findings.detail: While reserves improved to £10.324m, the council explicitly states the improvement includes £1.489m brought forward from prior year, plus a VAT refund and additional grants. These are one-off items. The council warns: 'The budget position therefore remains challenging, and pressures are arising for 2026/27.'
findings.matters: The headline figure obscures structural budget gaps that will persist, requiring service reductions or new revenue sources in coming years.
findings.figures: £1.935m improvement, but £1.489m from prior year carry forward plus non-recurring grants; reserves now £10.324m
findings.quote: a large element of the underspends are one off in year moves, from the release of carry forward budgets, the receipt of a VAT refund and additional grant. The budget position therefore remains challenging, and pressures are arising for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 260713 RG RBM Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: ICT infrastructure reserve now insufficient for lifecycle costs across the MTFP
findings.detail: ICT costs overspent by £0.711m in year, with £0.685m deterioration from Q3. The council budgeted to fund these costs from a dedicated ICT Infrastructure reserve, but that reserve is now fully committed to covering ongoing lifecycle needs, leaving no contingency buffer.
findings.matters: Underfunded technology infrastructure creates hidden future liabilities and suggests deferred visibility of IT system decay that could impact service delivery or compliance.
findings.figures: £0.711m ICT overspend, £0.685m increase from Q3
findings.quote: This is due to ICT infrastructure costs and inflationary cost increases, which were planned to be funded through the ICT Infrastructure reserve, however this reserve is required to cover the increased cost of ICT infrastructure across the life of the MTFP.

findings.paper_title: 260713 RG RBM Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Property fund investment income terminated, removing a source of recurring revenue
findings.detail: The council had been receiving investment income from a property fund but withdrew from it in 2025/26. This eliminated an ongoing revenue source, contributing to a £0.834m overspend in financing costs and indicating tighter future cash generation.
findings.matters: Loss of investment income signals the council is tightening its balance sheet and increases reliance on service-based funding and borrowing to balance budgets.
findings.figures: £0.834m overspend in financing costs, £0.642m increase from Q3 due to property fund income ending
findings.quote: Financing Costs for the year have overspent by £0.834m, an increase of £0.642m from Q3. This is due to a decrease in property fund income following the ending of the Council's investment

findings.paper_title: 260713 RG RBM Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Adoption and Placements overspent by £4.465m, driven by five new residential placements and complex needs support
findings.detail: The children's service overspent significantly in 2025/26, with £0.216m from new residential placements and £0.206m from additional support for complex needs and fee increases. This represents a £0.270m deterioration from Q3, indicating demand is still growing rather than stabilizing.
findings.matters: Children's placements are a core statutory obligation and rising costs indicate increasing vulnerability in the population; a lender needs to understand this demand trajectory.
findings.figures: £4.465m overspend, £0.216m new placements, £0.206m complex needs and fees, up £0.270m from Q3
findings.quote: Adoption and Placements has overspent by £4.465m, an increase of £0.270m from the Q3 report. This is due to five new residential placements costing £0.216m and a combination of additional support required to meet complex needs, and fee increases totalling £0.206m.

findings.paper_title: 260702 O + S Project Position Statement and Capital Programme Monitoring Outturn 25-26
findings.headline: Skinnergate Housing re-development flagged red for programme delays
findings.detail: The project has experienced multiple delays reported previously. Current status shows the remaining demolition phase is nearing completion, indicating some improvement.
findings.matters: Capital project delays affect service delivery schedules and cash flow forecasting, though the improving status suggests this is being managed
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: This project is flagged as red for programme due to a number of delays that have occurred on this project and have been reported previously. The remaining phase of demolition is now nearing completion.

findings.paper_title: 260702 O + S Project Position Statement and Capital Programme Monitoring Outturn 25-26
findings.headline: Hopetown Darlington capital project has unresolved cost dispute with Network Rail and worst-case 2% budget overrun
findings.detail: The project is showing a worst-case scenario overspend of 2%, with unresolved areas of dispute involving Network Rail costs. The council is seeking legal advice and engaging with Network Rail, with the process described as having potential to be protracted and uncertain.
findings.matters: Unresolved third-party disputes on capital schemes risk further cost escalations and additional borrowing needs, making cash flow unpredictable
findings.figures: 2% overspend worst-case scenario
findings.quote: The PPS is showing the worst-case scenario which represents an overspend of 2%. We are seeking legal advice on the areas of dispute and continuing to engage with Network Rail on costs. This has the potential to be a protracted process.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report and Outturn Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Interest rates expected to remain at 3.75% but carry upside risk if inflation accelerates further
findings.detail: Bank Rate is expected to remain flat at 3.75% through 2026/27, but the Treasury advisors note 'there could also be the possibility of increases should inflation start to rise' and flag that 'energy costs could see CPI inflation breach 4.5% later this year'. This creates uncertainty around the cost of any new borrowing or debt refinancing.
findings.matters: If rates rise, Darlington's strategy of under-borrowing against reserves becomes more costly — higher borrowing rates when the council is eventually forced to refinance will accelerate reserve depletion and compound the financing cost pressures already evident.
findings.figures: Bank Rate 3.75%; potential CPI inflation to 4.5%
findings.quote: The market now expects the bank rate to remain fairly static throughout 2026/27 due to uncertainty with the global economy and the impact this could have on inflation. There could also be the possibility of increases should inflation start to rise.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report and Outturn Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Council maintains £73.790m under-borrowed position using internal reserves — explicitly flagged as unsustainable
findings.detail: The Council finances its £249.881m Capital Financing Requirement with only £176.091m external debt, leaving a £73.790m 'under-borrowed' gap funded by internal cash reserves. The report states this strategy 'has served well over the last few years' but explicitly acknowledges it is 'kept under review to avoid incurring higher borrowing costs in the future when this authority may not be able to avoid new borrowing'. This signals recognition that reserves cannot sustain this indefinitely.
findings.matters: Reserve-funded borrowing is a finite strategy. When reserves deplete, the council will face forced external borrowing at market rates, potentially at higher cost. This creates an implicit refinancing cliff and constrains future financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Under-borrowed position £73.790m; external debt £167.597m vs CFR £249.881m
findings.quote: The policy of avoiding new borrowing by running down spare cash balances has served well over the last few years (see table 6 below). However, this was kept under review to avoid incurring higher borrowing costs in the future when this authority may not be able to avoid new borrowing to finance capital expenditure and/or the refinancing of maturing debt.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report and Outturn Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital expenditure slipped £17.603m below plan, concentrated in HRA and Towns Fund schemes
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure was £49.479m against a revised estimate of £65.944m. The slippage reduced the council's borrowing need from £17.786m to £10.321m. Most of the underperformance was in HRA capital projects and Towns Fund initiatives, suggesting delays in key service investment and regeneration programmes.
findings.matters: Significant capital underperformance signals programme delivery challenges. It also masks the true size of future borrowing needs — slipped schemes will need to be delivered in 2026/27, creating a lumpy capital profile.
findings.figures: £49.479m actual vs £65.944m budgeted; variance £17.603m; borrowing need reduced from £17.786m to £10.321m
findings.quote: Actual expenditure was £17.603m less than planned, mostly down to slippage in the HRA, and Towns Fund initiatives.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report and Outturn Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: £8.896m property fund distribution forced into debt repayment, eliminating long-term investment income
findings.detail: The Hermes Federated property fund merged and the Council, as a non-pension fund, could not transfer and instead received £8.896m in cash which was used to repay maturing debt. Additionally, property fund dividends fell from £0.927m budgeted to £0.671m actual due to fund terminations. This eliminates a source of passive income and forces reliance on debt reduction or reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Property funds provide steady investment returns to offset borrowing costs. Their loss means reduced treasury income and forces the council to pursue more aggressive reserve management or debt repayment strategies.
findings.figures: £8.896m Hermes cash distribution; property fund dividends £0.927m budgeted vs £0.671m actual (£0.256m shortfall)
findings.quote: The Council therefore received a cash distribution of £8.896m as it's share of the fund. This funding has been used to repay debt that was maturing in the short term to save on interest costs whilst options for longer term investments are investigated.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report and Outturn Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Financing costs increased £0.834m and now consume 4.51% of net revenue expenditure, up from 3.91%
findings.detail: Despite lower average borrowing rates (3.37% to 3.34%), financing costs overran budget by £0.834m. The increase is driven by loss of property fund dividends following the Hermes fund termination and reprofiling of MRP charges for Feethams House. Financing costs as a percentage of net revenue expenditure rose from 3.91% to 4.51% year-on-year, indicating underlying cost pressures.
findings.matters: Rising financing costs consume more of the council's annual revenue budget. The trend is concerning because it shows cost pressure despite lower borrowing rates, suggesting structural issues rather than temporary fluctuations.
findings.figures: £0.834m overspend; 3.91% to 4.51% of net revenue expenditure
findings.quote: Financing costs had an overspend of £0.834m due to a decrease in property fund dividends following the ending of one of the Council's investments and the reprofiling of Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charges and repayments for Feethams House following the 2024/25 budget outturn.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement Audit Committee Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: Council operating under Department for Education Safety Valve intervention for high needs spending pressures
findings.detail: Darlington entered into a Safety Valve agreement in March 2023 requiring development of substantial plans to place high needs systems on a sustainable footing. The agreement, which acknowledges pressures from special education and SEND deficits, remains in place until 2027.
findings.matters: High needs spending deficits and DfE intervention signal structural demand pressures in special education that the council must manage; failure to meet intervention targets could trigger further regulatory action.
findings.figures: Agreement from March 2023 through 2027
findings.quote: Darlington entered into an agreement in March 2023, that remains in place until 2027

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement Audit Committee Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: External auditors flag use of reserves to balance budget as unsustainable long-term
findings.detail: Forvis Mazars identified that relying on reserves to balance the budget is not sustainable and recommended the council identify other initiatives to achieve financial sustainability, depending on government funding outcomes.
findings.matters: The external auditor's assessment that the current budget model is unsustainable signals structural financial problems that cannot be solved by drawing down reserves; the council must identify service cuts or revenue increases.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: they highlighted the use of reserves to balance the Council's budget as not sustainable in the long term and recommended that the Council will need to consider other initiatives, depending on the outcome of the financial settlement from Government

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement Audit Committee Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: Council reserves will be completely exhausted by 2028/29 financial year
findings.detail: The council has a balanced budget through 2027/28 by drawing down reserves, but these reserves will be fully utilised by 2028/29. This leaves the council with no financial buffer and requires structural budget changes after that date.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion indicates the council cannot sustain current spending from revenues and must either cut services or increase income significantly; it also removes any cushion for unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls.
findings.figures: 2028/29 is the year reserves are fully used
findings.quote: The Council has a balanced budget up until 2027/28 using reserves, however reserves will be fully utilised during the 2028/29 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement Audit Committee Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: External auditors issuing disclaimed opinion on 2024/25 accounts
findings.detail: Forvis Mazars cannot complete full audits of all previous disclaimed opinions before the 27 February 2026 backstop date and will therefore report a disclaimed opinion on the 2024/25 accounts. This means the auditors cannot provide assurance on the council's financial position for the year.
findings.matters: Unaudited accounts prevent lenders from having reliable assurance on the council's financial position and create uncertainty about asset valuations, liabilities, and net worth.
findings.figures: Backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: the Council's external auditors Forvis Mazars are expected to report a disclaimed opinion on the Council's 2024/25 accounts to Audit Committee on 23 February ahead of the backstop date of 27 February 2026

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Darlington Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL ISSUED VERSION - UPDATED v2
findings.headline: Auditor raised 'other recommendation' that Council cannot allow itself to use all reserves and may need 'difficult decisions'
findings.detail: Although not classified as a significant weakness, the auditor recommended that the Council must manage its financial position carefully to minimize reserve contributions, particularly in Children's Services. The auditor explicitly stated: 'The Council cannot allow itself to use all of its reserves and may need to take difficult decisions if the position does not improve.'
findings.matters: This is the auditor's warning that the Council is on an unsustainable path and difficult cost/service reductions are imminent if circumstances do not change.
findings.figures: £34m earmarked reserves mostly committed; £16.4m available revenue reserves; forecast depletion 2027/28
findings.quote: The Council needs to consider some of the initiatives it has identified to address the underlying deficit and prevent a further draw on reserves to balance the budget. The Council cannot allow itself to use all of its reserves and may need to take 'difficult' decisions if the position does not improve.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Darlington Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL ISSUED VERSION - UPDATED v2
findings.headline: Three control deficiencies identified, including non-compliance with own asset policy and CIPFA guidance on depreciation
findings.detail: Auditors identified that the Council is not following its own policy on componentising significant assets, and is not following revised CIPFA infrastructure guidance. Assets are depreciated over a historic 30-year rate with no disaggregation by category. Member declarations of interest are not retained as evidence of annual review. None are rated as 'significant deficiencies' but all imply weak asset management controls.
findings.matters: Failure to follow own policies and accounting guidance means property and asset values may be materially misstated. Infrastructure depreciation is a material item and if calculated incorrectly, the accounts are unreliable.
findings.figures: Member declarations: majority signed 2021-2023; Infrastructure depreciation: 30-year historic rate with no CIPFA disaggregation
findings.quote: The Council's policy is to componentise significant assets but currently only a small number of assets are componentised. These include a number of assets which have been revalued in the year where new component data has not been provided by the external valuer.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Darlington Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL ISSUED VERSION - UPDATED v2
findings.headline: 2026/27 and beyond shows budget gaps despite settlement improvement, with no clear path back to balance
findings.detail: The 2026/27 MTFP projects budget gaps of circa £5.4m in 2026/27 and £2.5m in 2027/28, even after a 14.9% increase in core spending power and 4.99% council tax rises. These gaps can be 'fully covered' by unallocated reserves, but this further depletes the already-critical reserve position. The Council is hopeful that an 'economic growth plan' will help but this is not yet proven.
findings.matters: A council cannot bridge structural budget gaps indefinitely with reserves. Once reserves are gone, it faces impossible choices between cutting services and breaching statutory duties. The growth plan is speculative.
findings.figures: In-year budget gap 2026/27: £5.4m; 2027/28: £2.5m; Core spending power increase 2025/26 to 2028/29: 14.9%; Council tax increase assumed: 4.99% annually; Anticipated surpluses from 2028/29 onwards
findings.quote: When combined with an increase in Council Tax of 4.99% for each year (including the social care precept) and after additional pressures and savings, there will be an in year budget gap of circa £5.4m in 2026/27, £2.5m in 2027/28 and then an anticipated surpluses in 2028/29

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Darlington Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL ISSUED VERSION - UPDATED v2
findings.headline: Children's Services is running recurrent overspends of £3-4m annually with no resolution in sight
findings.detail: Children's Services overspent by £4.394m in 2023/24, £3.061m in 2022/23, and projects £4.352m overspend in 2025/26, mainly due to adoption and placement budgets. The auditor notes this is a regional and national issue but that it remains 'a significant financial pressure for the Council across the MTFP' with no apparent control or solution, beyond the Council lobbying government.
findings.matters: Recurrent overspends of this scale consume reserves and crowd out other services. Three years of overspend demonstrates it is structural, not temporary.
findings.figures: 2022/23: £3.061m overspend; 2023/24: £4.394m overspend; 2025/26 projected: £4.352m overspend; adoption and placement budget overspend 2025/26: £4.117m
findings.quote: The Quarter two financial monitoring report for 2025/26 was taken to Cabinet in November 2025. The main area of overspending in 2025/26 relates to Childrens' Services with a projected overspend of £4.352 million – mainly due to the adoption and placement budget overspend of £4.117 million. There were also significant overspends in the previous two years (2023/24 £4.394m, 2022/23 £3.061m).

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Darlington Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL ISSUED VERSION - UPDATED v2
findings.headline: General fund reserves forecast to be depleted by 2027/28, with ongoing structural budget deficits
findings.detail: General fund balances fell from £13.777m to £9.209m in 2024/25 alone. The Council's own forecasts show general fund balances will be fully exhausted by 2027/28. The 2024/25 MTFP originally forecast £34.1m in reserve contributions up to 2027/28, but the Council only has circa £16.4m of revenue reserves available (excluding earmarked reserves). The Council is operating with an underlying deficit requiring significant draws on reserves each year.
findings.matters: A council cannot operate without reserves. Depletion below minimum levels creates acute financial vulnerability and constrains the council's ability to respond to shocks or meet statutory duties.
findings.figures: General fund balances: £13.777m (2024) → £9.209m (2025); Earmarked reserves: £46.528m → £34.192m; Total usable reserves reduced £16.906m; Available revenue reserves ~£16.4m; Forecast depletion 2027/28
findings.quote: The Council only has circa £16.4 million of reserves to support the revenue budget (including a £5.350 million risk reserve within earmarked reserves and circa £1.5 million group joint profits). The 2024/25 MTFP forecasted that general fund balances would be fully depleted by 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Darlington Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL ISSUED VERSION - UPDATED v2
findings.headline: Material error identified in land and buildings valuations, already corrected but audit work in this area incomplete
findings.detail: Auditors found a material error in the Council's property valuations and it was amended in the financial statements. However, work on this significant risk area was not completed before the accounts were finalized, leaving potential for further undetected issues.
findings.matters: Property represents a material balance sheet item. An incomplete audit on valuations means the adjusted figure may still contain errors.
findings.figures: Material adjusted misstatement identified; specific amount not disclosed in auditor sections
findings.quote: We have identified a material error in the Council's valuations of land and buildings and this has been amended in the financial statements as set out in section 06 of this report. We were unable to finish our work in this audit area before the accounts were finalised.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Darlington Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL ISSUED VERSION - UPDATED v2
findings.headline: Auditors halted work mid-audit because accounts were finalized and could not be amended if problems were found
findings.detail: Auditors stopped working on 2024/25 accounts before completing all procedures because the final version was prepared for approval and there was no scope to further amend accounts if issues were identified. They planned to work until 27 February 2026 but stopped earlier out of concern they might find material changes that could not be made.
findings.matters: This means critical audit areas were not fully tested: management override of controls, pensions valuations, and lease accounting remain incomplete. Issues may exist but will not be resolved.
findings.figures: Backstop date 27 February 2026; work stopped before completion
findings.quote: we have stopped working on the 2024/25 accounts. This is because the final version of the accounts has been prepared for approval by Members and there is no scope to further amend the accounts if we identify additional issues

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Darlington Borough Council - Audit Completion Report 2024-25 - FINAL ISSUED VERSION - UPDATED v2
findings.headline: The Council will receive a third consecutive disclaimed audit opinion and audit work remains incomplete
findings.detail: Darlington received a disclaimed opinion in 2022/23, could not complete 2023/24, and will issue another disclaimer for 2024/25. Auditors stopped work before completing all procedures, unable to rebuild assurance in time for the 27 February 2026 backstop date. The 'Proof in Total' methodology for rebuilding assurance was not available for 2024/25.
findings.matters: Three years without an audited opinion means the financial statements are unvetted and the Council's financial position is not independently verified. Lenders cannot rely on audited accounts.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions issued 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25 backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: we were not able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide a basis for an audit opinion on these financial statements before the 2026 backstop date

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG Council Prudential Indicators and Treasury Management Strategy Report 2026-27
findings.headline: New borrowing to incur revenue cost due to cost of carry — borrowing rates exceed investment returns.
findings.detail: The council maintains an under-borrowed position (£56.7m underborrowed in 2026/27) as a deliberate strategy, expecting interest rates to fall. However, the strategy creates immediate budget pressure: any borrowing needed to fund capital or debt maturities will cost more to borrow than the council can earn on cash deposits, creating a revenue drag.
findings.matters: Cost of carry is a quantified revenue budget pressure. If interest rates do not fall as forecast, the council will carry higher debt service costs for years. This affects affordability of both capital and revenue spending.
findings.quote: While the Council will not be able to avoid borrowing to finance new capital expenditure, to replace maturing debt and the rundown of reserves, there will be a cost of carry (the difference between higher borrowing costs and lower investment returns), so any new short or medium-term borrowing will incur a revenue cost.

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG Council Prudential Indicators and Treasury Management Strategy Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Property fund portfolio of £16m acknowledged to have decreased in capital value; one fund winding down by May 2026.
findings.detail: The council's property fund investments have declined from £25.318m in March 2025 to £16m by December 2025 due to economic conditions. The Lothbury property fund is in final wind-down, closing May 2026. The council expects recovery of capital values, but explicitly notes this depends on economic climate.
findings.matters: Unrealised losses on property fund holdings hit the balance sheet under IFRS 9. Fund wind-down creates liquidity needs and concentration risk in remaining two funds. Recovery assumption is conditional on macroeconomic conditions.
findings.figures: March 2025: £25.318m; December 2025: £16m; 2024/25 dividend income: £0.981m
findings.quote: Capital values of property funds do fluctuate over time and due to prevailing economic conditions over the past few years the capital value of our invetments has decreased. During 2025/26 we have seen capital values start to recover as interest rates and inflation start to fall.

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG Council Prudential Indicators and Treasury Management Strategy Report 2026-27
findings.headline: HRA financing costs ratio spiking to 14.07% in 2026/27, up 158 basis points year-on-year.
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account's ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream jumps from 12.49% in 2025/26 to 14.07% in 2026/27 before easing back to 12.51% in 2027/28. This temporary spike concentrates debt service costs into a single year without explanation in this document.
findings.matters: HRA is self-financing and highly sensitive to cost pressures. A spike in financing costs as a share of revenue signals affordability stress and could constrain housing investment or require rent increases.
findings.quote: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream – HRA: 12.49%, 14.07%, 12.51%, 12.62%

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG Council Prudential Indicators and Treasury Management Strategy Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Loans to joint ventures increasing to £20.1m in 2026/27, a four-fold increase from £4.6m.
findings.detail: Capital expenditure plan includes £20.114m in loans to joint ventures for 2026/27, up sharply from £4.590m in 2025/26, with £33.654m of JV loans embedded in the Capital Financing Requirement by 2026/27. These are classified as commercial loans and require mandatory Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charges against revenue until fully repaid.
findings.matters: Large expansion of council lending to third parties increases contingent liabilities and revenue burden through mandatory MRP charges. Lenders need visibility on what ventures are being funded and their return profile.
findings.quote: The Authority's loans to joint ventures are categorised as commercial loans. It should be noted however that the loan repayments can also be used to reduce the CFR and hence the MRP charge, however, until the loan has been fully repaid MRP must be charged.

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG Housing Revenue Account (HRA)
findings.headline: Multiple new regulatory requirements introduced with unquantified cost implications: Fire Safety regulations, Awaab's Law, and new Decent Homes Standards
findings.detail: The council faces compliance obligations from Fire Safety regulations (2022) requiring replacement of all doors in blocks and communal schemes; Awaab's Law (October 2025) requiring priority response to damp and mould; and new Consumer Standards from the Regulator of Social Housing (April 2024). These are referenced as drivers of cost pressures, but the specific costs are not fully quantified in the MTFP.
findings.matters: Unquantified regulatory compliance costs represent a contingent liability. If these costs exceed projections, they will further strain the HRA budget at a time when reserves are already declining.
findings.figures: Fire doors required in blocks of flats and communal schemes over 'next few years'; Awaab's Law implemented October 2025; Consumer Standards introduced April 2024. Window and door replacement budget 2026-27: £2.025m (includes fire doors).
findings.quote: Awaab's Law, introduced in October 2025, also requires social landlords to address damp and mould reports with higher priority and new Fire Safety regulations introduced in 2022 also require us to replace all our doors in blocks of flats and communal housing schemes over the next few years.

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG Housing Revenue Account (HRA)
findings.headline: Service charges increasing sharply in some categories, notably building cleaning up 37.9% and meals up 20%, amplifying tenant cost pressures
findings.detail: Proposed service charge increases vary widely. Building cleaning for flats increases 37.9% (£2.82 to £3.89/week); sheltered building cleaning up 24.9%; extra care meals increase 20% (£58.43 to £70.14/week); Housing Plus Service up 13.1%. The council states these subsidies are being 'phased out' but the scale of increases, particularly for vulnerable groups in sheltered and extra care schemes, will add to financial strain.
findings.matters: These increases, layered on top of the 4.8% rent increase, will disproportionately affect vulnerable tenants and are likely to worsen rent collection. The council notes that approx. 70% of tenants receive Housing Benefit or Universal Credit, but gaps between these benefits and total housing costs will widen.
findings.figures: Building Cleaning Flats: 37.9% (£2.82 → £3.89); Sheltered cleaning: 24.9% (£5.15 → £6.43); Extra Care meals: 20% (£58.43 → £70.14); Housing Plus: 13.1% (£22.90 → £25.90). Approx. 70% of tenants eligible for Housing Benefit/Universal Credit.
findings.quote: Building Cleaning – Flats 2.82 3.89 37.9%... Mid-day Meal – Extra Care (Residents Only) 58.43 70.14 20.0%... Housing Plus Service 22.90 25.90 13.1%

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG Housing Revenue Account (HRA)
findings.headline: Tenant affordability stress: 72% of tenants surveyed opposed the rent increase; 30% reported difficulty paying rent
findings.detail: Consultation on the 4.8% rent increase saw 1,296 responses (24.9% of tenants, up 44% from previous year). Of these, 72% disagreed with the increase. Main reasons cited were cost of living (43%), the increase being too high (20%), struggling to pay current rent (15%), and properties not maintained (11%). Additionally, 30% of respondents reported having had problems paying rent over the past year, and 55% contacted the council about struggling to pay.
findings.matters: High levels of tenant opposition and documented payment difficulties increase the risk of rent arrears and bad debts. The council budgets £263k for bad debt provision, but widespread affordability stress could exceed this reserve.
findings.figures: Survey responses: 1,296 (24.9% of 5,266 tenants); Opposition: 72%; Cost of living cited: 43%; Had payment difficulties: 30%; Contacted council for help: 55%; Bad debt provision: £263k.
findings.quote: Do you think the proposed rent increase is reasonable?  Yes = 28% and No = 72%.  The main reasons given were the cost of living (43%), the proposed rent increase is too high (20%), struggling to pay the current rent (15%), and properties are not kept up to date (11%).

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG Housing Revenue Account (HRA)
findings.headline: £8.2m of new prudential borrowing required in 2026-27 to fund the new build programme
findings.detail: The council plans to borrow an additional £8.2m in 2026-27 for new build Council housing and energy efficiency, funded through capital receipts from Right to Buy sales, Homes England grants (approximately 30% of costs), and prudential borrowing. This is on top of existing capital financing costs of £4.833m annually.
findings.matters: Lenders need to monitor the council's debt trajectory. The council has stated this is self-financing over the life of new build schemes, but the scale of new borrowing in a single year, combined with declining reserves, requires assessment of debt capacity.
findings.figures: Additional borrowing 2026-27: £8.238m; Existing capital financing costs: £4.833m; Homes England grant assumption: ~30% of new build costs; 365 homes already delivered, 108 under construction.
findings.quote: Since the abolition of the HRA borrowing cap, we have been able to prudentially borrow and have included estimated additional borrowing of £8.2m in 2026-27 to build new affordable homes and contribute to energy efficiency.

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG Housing Revenue Account (HRA)
findings.headline: £32m energy efficiency gap: 2,350 homes need upgrades to meet 2030 EPC C requirement, but the council has funded only £13.9m of investment
findings.detail: The council has approximately 2,350 properties that do not meet the Government's Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) C rating, which must be addressed by 2030. Current estimates put the full cost at £32m (approximately £12.8k per property). The council has only committed £13.9m to upgrade around 1,000 homes over the next 3 years through HRA investment plus £3.5m in external grant funding.
findings.matters: This is a regulatory deadline with a material shortfall in funding. The council acknowledges 'significantly more investment will be required' but has no identified source for the gap, creating uncertainty about compliance.
findings.figures: 2,350 non-compliant properties; £32m estimated cost; £12.8k per property; £13.9m planned 3-year investment; £3.5m grant funding.
findings.quote: We have approx. 2,350 properties that don't meet the Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) C rating which will need to be addressed by 2030. We don't know the full costs yet, but current estimates, based on stock condition data, suggest the amount to be around £32m, which is approx. £12.8k for each property. However, significantly more investment will be required to meet Government targets.

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG Housing Revenue Account (HRA)
findings.headline: Repairs and maintenance costs have jumped 50% in three years, outpacing inflation significantly
findings.detail: Darlington's repairs and maintenance costs rose from £4.759m in 2021-22 to £7.153m in 2024-25. The council attributes this to countrywide pressure on building materials and contractor costs increasing above inflation. This ongoing cost escalation is driving the need for the 4.8% rent increase despite tenant financial pressures.
findings.matters: Cost pressures this severe raise questions about whether the HRA budget is built on sustainable assumptions, and indicate the council may face further pressures if construction costs continue to rise.
findings.figures: Repairs costs: £4.759m (2021-22) → £7.153m (2024-25); 50% increase in 3 years. 2026-27 budget: £7.455m.
findings.quote: For example, our Repairs and Maintenance costs have increased from £4.759m in 2021-22 to £7.153m in 2024-25, a 50% increase in 3 years.

findings.paper_title: Setting the Council Tax for 2026-27
findings.headline: £0.870m Collection Fund deficit to be covered from reserves
findings.detail: The council estimates a £1.048m deficit on the Collection Fund at 31 March 2026, with Darlington's share being £0.870m. This shortfall will be covered from the Collection Fund reserve rather than being recouped from future years' income.
findings.matters: A Collection Fund deficit indicates the council collected less council tax than projected. Drawing reserves to cover this reduces financial flexibility and signals below-budget income collection.
findings.figures: £1.048m total deficit; £0.870m Darlington's share
findings.quote: It is estimated that there will be a £1.048m deficit on the Collection Fund at 31st March 2026. Darlington's proportion of this is £0.870m and will be covered from the Collection Fund reserve.

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG MTFP
findings.headline: Financial sustainability from 2028/29 depends on Fair Funding Reform delivering and house building growth of 1.25% annually
findings.detail: The plan shows a surplus from 2028/29 onwards, but paragraph 96 explicitly warns of 'significant degree of uncertainty about the future economic position'. The council assumes 461 Band D equivalent new properties annually; if house building slips, Council Tax growth assumptions fail and deficits continue.
findings.matters: The assumed rebalancing is not due to spending cuts — it assumes external funding and growth materialise. If they don't, the council faces continued structural deficits with no remaining reserves.
findings.figures: 14.9% CSP increase from Fair Funding Reform; 1.25% annual tax base growth assumed; projections show return to surplus 2028/29
findings.quote: Notwithstanding this there is a significant degree of uncertainty about the future economic position and demand for services so the position presented whilst as accurate as possible will change, however at this conjuncture I cannot be sure if that will be for the better or worse.

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG MTFP
findings.headline: Financing costs rising £0.801m in 2026/27 due to sustained higher interest rates constraining capital programme
findings.detail: Interest rates remain 'higher levels than previously forecast', increasing borrowing costs for capital schemes such as the Dolphin Centre refurbishment. Additionally, closure of a council property fund has reduced dividend income. These pressures directly reduce revenue available for services.
findings.matters: Rising refinancing costs reduce financial headroom. They constrain the council's ability to borrow for regeneration schemes, which are a key strategy for revenue growth through business rates.
findings.figures: £0.801m pressure in 2026/27 due to higher interest rates
findings.quote: the largest is financing costs with a pressure of £0.801m in 2026/27. This is due to interest rates remaining at higher levels than previously forecast, which impacts on the cost of borrowing for new capital schemes such as the Dolphin Centre refurbishment.

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG MTFP
findings.headline: Hopetown income-generating scheme is £0.705m below business case in 2026/27 (£1.855m across plan)
findings.detail: The Hopetown facility is underperforming its original income assumptions. The council notes it is 'being undertaken with a view to mitigating these pressures' — indicating the underperformance is still being remediated, not solved.
findings.matters: Shows a capital-dependent income stream is not delivering. Signals either that business case assumptions were flawed or market conditions have deteriorated. This pattern affects debt service capacity.
findings.figures: £0.705m shortfall in 2026/27; £1.855m across MTFP
findings.quote: the main area affecting this category is Hopetown where the anticipated income is £0.705m lower than the original business case in 2026/27 and £1.855m across the MTFP. A full review of the Hopetown business case is being undertaken with a view to mitigating these pressures over the MTFP period.

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG MTFP
findings.headline: Children's Social Care pressures of £10.618m over the plan period are not fully resolved by transformation
findings.detail: The council reports a 50% increase in agency contacts, 45% increase in referrals, and 11% increase in children in care since pre-pandemic. The largest pressure is residential placements for complex cases, which the council describes as 'a fundamental and nationwide issue regarding the availability and cost of children's residential placements'. This is a statutory service consuming one-third of the budget.
findings.matters: These are mandatory costs the council cannot refuse. The ongoing increases in complex cases suggest the problem is structural, not cyclical, and existing management interventions may not be sufficient.
findings.figures: £3.928m pressure in 2026/27; £10.618m across MTFP; 50% increase in contacts, 45% increase in referrals, 11% increase in children in care
findings.quote: We are seeing more vulnerable children with increasingly complex needs requiring help and support; last year we saw a 50% increase in contacts from partner agencies and people concerned for a child's welfare, a 45% increase in referrals and an 11% increase in children in our care since pre pandemic levels.

findings.paper_title: 260219 RG MTFP
findings.headline: Usable reserves depleted from £9.787m to £3.597m in two years to cover structural deficits
findings.detail: The council requires drawing £5.404m from reserves in 2026/27 and £2.486m in 2027/28 to balance the budget. After these withdrawals, usable reserves fall to £3.597m by 2027/28 — a 63% reduction. The council explicitly states the position 'is fragile and reliant on the funding reform predictions'.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves remove the financial buffer for unforeseen social care demand spikes or cost overruns. The plan's rebalancing depends on transformation programmes landing in 2028/29.
findings.figures: Opening balance £9.787m; closing 2027/28 £3.597m; deficits of £5.404m (2026/27) and £2.486m (2027/28)
findings.quote: We are anticipating having £9.787m reserves which can be utilised to support the plan over that period, however, it is clear the financial position is fragile and reliant on the funding reform predictions, along with Council Tax increases to ensure sustainability.

news_drafts.headline: Council writing off £1.22 million of irrecoverable debts across all revenue streams
news_drafts.lead: High write-off volumes indicate a significant proportion of assessed debts are unrecoverable, reducing effective revenue collection and potentially signalling deteriorating creditworthiness of the local population or businesses.
news_drafts.paper_title: 260713 Collection of Council Tax, Business Rates and Rent 2025-26

news_drafts.headline: Sundry debts outstanding jumped £3.2 million to £14.75 million with only 92.3% collection rate
news_drafts.lead: Growing sundry debt stock indicates accumulating receivables that may become irrecoverable; the 92.3% collection rate is significantly below Council Tax and Business Rates, suggesting service areas struggle to collect from customers.
news_drafts.paper_title: 260713 Collection of Council Tax, Business Rates and Rent 2025-26

news_drafts.headline: Council rent arrears grew 20% to £1.06 million due to structural shift from Housing Benefit to Universal Credit
news_drafts.lead: This is a structural, ongoing issue not temporary economic weakness. The UC payment cycle creates a permanent arrears bulge that will require ongoing collection effort and may require housing revenue account provisions.
news_drafts.paper_title: 260713 Collection of Council Tax, Business Rates and Rent 2025-26
